title: Pontius Pilate
lead: The Roman prefect of Judea from about AD 26 to 36, who ordered Jesus' crucifixion. He is known from the Gospels, Philo, Josephus, Tacitus and an inscription found at Caesarea, and is named in the Christian creeds.

sections.b: Pilate governed Judea under the emperor Tiberius. A building inscription found at Caesarea Maritima in 1961 calls him "prefect of Judea." Philo, writing in his lifetime, describes him as stubborn, harsh and corrupt (On the Embassy to Gaius 299–305). Josephus tells how he brought images of the emperor into Jerusalem, used Temple money for an aqueduct, and was removed after a massacre of Samaritans (Jewish War 2.169–177; Antiquities 18.55–89). Tacitus records that Christ was executed under him (Annals 15.44). Luke 13:1 mentions Galileans "whose blood Pilate mixed with their sacrifices."
sections.refs: Luke 3:1; Luke 13:1; Matthew 27:2; John 18:28–19:22; Acts 4:27; 1 Timothy 6:13

sections.h: Pilate in the Gospels and in later tradition
sections.b: All four Gospels show Pilate questioning Jesus about being "King of the Jews," finding no fault, offering Barabbas, and giving in to pressure. Many scholars see the Gospels' portrait as softer than Philo's and explain it by the churches' wish not to appear anti-Roman. Later Christian writings went further: the Acts of Pilate made him almost a believer, the Ethiopian Church honors him and his wife as saints, and the Coptic tradition once did; the Orthodox churches honor his wife, Procla. Western legend, by contrast, had him die in despair. The creed's "suffered under Pontius Pilate" fixes Jesus' death in real history.
